description: Never be Frog is a solo-team
summary:
Destello is a free, bilingual (English and Spanish) web tool that turns NASA SPHEREx all-sky infrared images into time-lapse animations of any patch of sky. Type coordinates or an object name and Destello finds every SPHEREx image of that position, groups them by survey epoch and detector, builds calibrated coadds and blinks them with one shared intensity stretch, so anything that moves or changes stands out. Users can subtract epochs, overlay Gaia and CatWISE sources propagated to each observation date, extract a spectrum, and measure the motion of a source.

Destello addresses the challenge by validating itself on the named targets with real data only. It measures the proper motion of Barnard's Star at 10,373 mas/yr against the published 10,399 mas/yr, recovers the motion of the cold brown dwarf WISE 0855, and detects the CO2 band of comet 3I/ATLAS. A public validation page reports 24 of 28 checks passing and states the failures and limits openly. Every frame is traceable to its source images, data release and DOI, every view is a shareable link, and a Hunt mode lets anyone inspect candidate fields. It lowers the barrier to searching for new nearby worlds.
details:
What it does

Destello takes a sky position (RA/Dec or a name resolved through CDS Sesame and SIMBAD), queries NASA/IPAC IRSA for every SPHEREx image covering it, clusters the images into survey epochs, subtracts the zodiacal light model, masks flagged pixels, reprojects and coadds per detector, and plays the epochs as a blink animation. Tools on top of the animation: difference images scaled by field-star flux, catalog overlays (Gaia DR3, CatWISE2020) propagated with proper motion and parallax to each frame's date, on-the-fly spectra using the spectral WCS of the linear variable filters, astrometric motion fits, a 16-year view that joins WISE and NEOWISE epochs to SPHEREx, a moving-target mode for comets with JPL Horizons ephemerides, and a Hunt mode where visitors review candidate fields.

How we know it works

A validation page lists 28 quantitative checks computed from real data: 24 pass, 2 fail and 2 are not measurable, each with its cause. Barnard's Star: 10,372.7 mas/yr measured, 10,398.6 published. WISE 0855: motion consistent with CatWISE2020. Comet 3I/ATLAS: CO2 band excess at 6.5 sigma. Tolerances were fixed before the measurements and were not adjusted.

Benefits and impact

Blinking images is how Pluto was found. Destello gives that method to anyone with a browser, on a new all-sky infrared survey, in two languages, with keyboard access, reduced-motion support and colorblind-safe palettes. Every frame records its source observation IDs, data release, DOI, detector and wavelength range, so a finding can be checked by others. Views are shareable URLs and can be embedded in any site, which suits classrooms and outreach.

Tools

Python 3.12, FastAPI, arq and Redis, astropy, astroquery, pyvo, photutils, reproject, numpy, scipy; React, TypeScript, Vite, TanStack Router and Query, Tailwind CSS, Aladin Lite, Plotly; Docker Compose, Caddy, an NGINX web application firewall with the OWASP rule set, Cloudflare, GitHub Actions. Code: https://github.com/felicabrera/destello (MIT).

What we considered

Scientific honesty first: no simulated or interpolated data, epoch-correct positions, one stretch per detector, limits stated in the interface (for example, Epsilon Indi Ba/Bb is unresolved at 6.2 arcsec pixels). Then security (no user-controlled outbound requests, allowlisted hosts) and resilience (a static demo with cached real data if the archive is unreachable).
